opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a tricky one, because I do think open-weight models have delivered a lot of value. They've been enormously useful for safety research in particular: you can't do serious interpretability work, or study fine-tuning attacks, or red-team a model properly, if you only have API access. So I don't want to throw that away. But we have to be honest that the safeguards we put on open models today are pretty shallow. Our own work and plenty of others' has shown that you can strip out refusal training with a small amount of fine-tuning, sometimes a few dozen examples and a few dollars of compute. So once the weights are out, the safety training is more of a suggestion than a guarantee.

I see a few promising directions. The first is moving the safety intervention earlier in the pipeline. Rather than training a model to know something dangerous and then refuse to talk about it, you filter the pretraining data so the model never acquires certain hazardous capabilities to begin with, say detailed knowledge relevant to bioweapons. It's much harder to fine-tune a capability back in from scratch than to undo a refusal, and early results suggest you can do this without hurting general performance much.

The second is tamper-resistant training: methods that make it costly to fine-tune a model toward harmful behavior, so the attacker has to spend something closer to the cost of training the capability themselves. This area is still immature. A lot of proposed defenses have been broken fairly quickly once people tried adaptive attacks, so I'd treat it as a research bet, not a solved problem, and I'd want third-party evaluations before anyone leans on it.

Third, and maybe most important, is being more deliberate about which capabilities go out openly and when. I don't think "open" versus "closed" has to be a binary. You can release a model openly once you've evaluated, after accounting for the realistic ways people will modify it, that its marginal uplift for really dangerous misuse is low. You can also do staged releases, or offer researcher access to frontier weights under some kind of agreement. That keeps most of the benefits for science and for the broader ecosystem while not handing over the most dangerous capabilities to everyone, irreversibly, on day one.

The key thing is that releasing weights is a one-way door. You can't recall a model. So the bar for evaluation should reflect that, and we should be testing open models against what a motivated adversary can do with them after fine-tuning, not just how they behave out of the box.

r001.rationale: The response says tamper-resistant training could make harmful fine-tuning costly, but does not say that removing refusals substantially degrades the model’s capabilities.

r002.rationale: It says an attacker may need to spend close to the cost of training the dangerous capability themselves, identifying training cost as a barrier to circumventing the defense.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention gradient routing or localizing dangerous capabilities within an expert.

r004.rationale: The response discusses staged releases and researcher access, but does not propose limiting distribution of a dangerous-capability expert to trusted actors.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest starting point is that there's a real tension here, and I don't want to pretend it away. Once weights are out, you can't recall them, and any safety training you've done can be fine-tuned off for a few hundred dollars of compute. We've shown that ourselves. So "make the open model itself robust" is, at least with current techniques, not really a solution.

But I don't think that means the answer is just "don't release anything." A lot of the safety research my team and others do depends on white-box access. You can't do good interpretability, you can't do rigorous adversarial testing, you can't study fine-tuning dynamics properly on a model you only hit through an API. So there's a genuine cost to closing everything down, and it's a cost that falls disproportionately on exactly the people trying to make these systems safer.

So where I land is something like a few overlapping approaches.

The first is being much more deliberate about the capability threshold. Right now the decision to open-weight a model is mostly a function of corporate strategy rather than any real assessment of marginal risk. I'd like to see a norm, and eventually probably a requirement, that before release you actually evaluate what the model adds in terms of uplift for things like bio or cyber, compared to what's already openly available. For most models today, that marginal uplift is pretty small, and I think releasing them is fine. The question is whether we'll keep applying that test honestly as capabilities go up, rather than just assuming it's always fine because it was fine last time.

The second is investing in techniques that actually make tamper resistance real. There's early work on making models harder to fine-tune in harmful directions, essentially trying to bake in safety at a deeper level than a thin layer of RLHF. I'm somewhat skeptical we get all the way there, but even raising the cost from hundreds of dollars to hundreds of thousands changes who can do it, and that matters.

And the third, which I think gets underrated, is structured access. There's a lot of space between "fully open on Hugging Face" and "chat API only." You can give vetted researchers access to weights under agreements, you can offer fine-tuning and activation access through a controlled environment, you can do staged releases where the research community gets it first and you watch what happens. That preserves most of the scientific value while keeping some ability to respond if something goes wrong. It's not as clean as full openness, and there are real questions about who does the vetting and whether it just entrenches the big labs. But I'd rather have those arguments than default into one of the two extremes.

So I guess my summary is: keep releasing at current capability levels, get serious about measuring marginal risk before releasing further, and build out the infrastructure for middle-ground access so that when we do hit a model that's too dangerous to just put out there, the safety community doesn't get locked out along with everyone else.

r001.rationale: It mentions making models harder to fine-tune in harmful directions, but does not say that removing refusals would substantially degrade the model’s capabilities.

r002.rationale: It discusses raising the cost of harmful fine-tuning, but does not identify training a model from scratch as a barrier.

r003.rationale: It does not mention gradient routing or localizing dangerous capabilities within an expert.

r004.rationale: It proposes structured access for vetted researchers, but does not propose limiting distribution of a dangerous-capability expert to trusted actors.

astra-6.text:
I think the goal should be to preserve people’s ability to study, modify, and build on these models while making harmful uses harder. And that means being clear about what kind of safety we’re getting. If you release the weights, you shouldn’t assume that a refusal trained into the model will survive someone deliberately fine-tuning it away.

So I’d put a lot of emphasis on evaluating the underlying capabilities before release. Does this model actually make a dangerous task substantially easier? How much expertise or compute would someone need to adapt it for that purpose? Those questions seem more informative than just asking whether the chatbot answers a harmful prompt.

There’s also a real opportunity to use openness to improve safety. Independent researchers can investigate failures, test defenses, and reproduce results. I’d like us to preserve that access, including in cases where unrestricted release might be too risky. A staged release or access for researchers could help us learn before making an irreversible decision.

I don’t think there’s a single technique that resolves the tension. The aim is to make release decisions based on evidence about particular risks, while treating broad access as something valuable that we should work to retain.

r001.rationale: The response says a refusal trained into a model may not survive deliberate fine-tuning, but does not describe tamper-resistant training or capability degradation when refusals are removed.

r002.rationale: It does not identify the expense of training from scratch as a barrier to circumventing refusals.

r003.rationale: It discusses evaluating model capabilities, but does not mention gradient routing or localizing dangerous capabilities in an expert.

r004.rationale: It mentions staged release and researcher access, but does not propose restricting a dangerous-capability expert to trusted actors.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to distinguish access to a model from confidence that it’s safe in a particular setting. I’m excited about open weights because they let researchers examine systems, find failures, and develop defenses without needing permission from a model provider. That can be a real advantage for safety.

But making the weights available doesn’t itself solve the safety problem. I’d like to see much stronger adversarial testing before release: not just whether the model behaves well on ordinary prompts, but whether someone actively trying to break its safeguards can do so. And then we need to make those findings useful—release evaluations, document limitations, and give people tools to test the defenses they’re building.

There’s also a distinction between releasing weights and how you deploy them. You might want fairly broad access to a model, while being much more careful about giving it credentials, access to sensitive data, or the ability to take consequential actions. Those deployment decisions matter enormously.

The difficult case is if a model has a dangerous capability that remains accessible after its safeguards are removed. With open weights, you have to assume someone can modify the model. So I don’t think we should promise that a refusal mechanism makes an otherwise dangerous release safe. The goal should be to preserve broad access wherever we can, while being honest about what our defenses actually withstand.

r001.rationale: The response calls for adversarial testing and cautions that safeguards can be removed, but does not describe refusal training that makes fine-tuning away refusals degrade capabilities.

r002.rationale: It does not identify the cost of training from scratch as a barrier to circumventing refusals.

r003.rationale: It does not mention gradient routing or localizing dangerous capabilities in a particular expert.

r004.rationale: It discusses restricting sensitive deployment access, but does not propose limiting distribution of a dangerous-capability expert to trusted actors.
